title: Effectiveness of non-pharmaceutical intervention on sperm quality: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
article_subtype: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
condition_or_topic: Male infertility and the effects of non-pharmaceutical interventions on sperm quality
clinical_background: Infertility is defined as failure to achieve pregnancy after twelve months or more of appropriately timed, unprotected intercourse. It affects approximately 10 to 15 percent of people worldwide; of approximately 186 million infertility cases, more than half involve male infertility. Reproductive-tract inflammation, lifestyle factors and nutritional deficiencies may contribute to impaired sperm quality. The article also reports that oxidative stress may contribute to about 30–80% of male infertility by damaging sperm components and function. Although non-pharmaceutical approaches have been used to manage male infertility, earlier reviews had not compared their relative effects.
objectives: Assess the effectiveness of non-pharmaceutical interventions on sperm quality.
Compare the effectiveness of non-pharmaceutical treatments for male infertility using a network meta-analysis.
clinical_question: In men with infertility (P), how do non-pharmaceutical interventions, including exercise, acupuncture and nutritional supplements (I), compare with placebo, mock acupuncture, no exercise or other interventions (C) for pregnancy rate and sperm concentration, total motility, forward motility, quality and count (O)?
interpretation: The authors interpret the network meta-analysis as showing benefits for several measures of male fertility. They report higher pregnancy rates with exercise, zinc and acupuncture; improved sperm concentration with acupuncture, ω-3 fatty acid, lycopene and vitamin; improved total sperm motility with acupuncture and lycopene; improved forward motility with acupuncture, lycopene and CoQ10; and a higher sperm count with lycopene. They also suggest that other dietary supplements may benefit male fertility. These conclusions concern semen parameters and pregnancy rates, while the direct effects of the interventions on fertility require further investigation.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors regard their observed association of exercise, zinc and acupuncture with higher clinical pregnancy rates as consistent with earlier studies of diet, exercise and acupuncture involving women. They cite prior work on the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of omega-3 fatty acids and on the importance of sperm-membrane lipids for fertilization; their finding on ω-3 fatty acid supplementation and sperm concentration accords with that work. They also cite earlier studies suggesting that acupuncture may reduce sperm lipid peroxidation or genital inflammation, and reports that CoQ10 may lessen oxidative stress in sperm cells. Prior research on carnitines and sperm motility, and on zinc, selenium and vitamin intake in relation to semen measures, is presented as context for their findings.
clinical_implications: The authors suggest that non-pharmaceutical interventions may improve semen parameters relevant to male infertility, although improved semen quality does not by itself establish a direct effect on fertility.

They describe acupuncture as a possible option for asthenospermia and state that findings on sperm concentration and motility support its possible use in patients with oligozoospermia or asthenospermia.
They caution that pregnancy rate depends on factors beyond sperm quality and should not serve as the principal index or gold standard for judging clinical effects in male infertility.
practice_implications: The authors propose considering acupuncture, exercise, dietary supplements and foods rich in the discussed supplements as non-pharmaceutical approaches for improving sperm-quality parameters and potentially influencing male fertility.
limitations: Some non-English publications could not be reviewed because translation into commonly used languages was unavailable; including their data might change the analyses.
Differences among study subgroups hindered an overall comparison. Excluding lower-quality studies and performing subgroup analyses only partly addressed this issue.
The direct effect of non-pharmaceutical interventions on fertility remains insufficiently studied, despite the reported improvements in sperm quality.
Multiple factors influence pregnancy rate, limiting its use as the main index or gold standard of clinical effect in male infertility.
Semen-testing reference standards differed between research units.
The range of male-infertility types and interventions created a need for further classification of the interventions.

Few studies of supplements and acupuncture were included, resulting in a small sample for those interventions; the authors also cite high heterogeneity and warn that additional research may change the effect estimates.
strengths: The authors describe this as their most extensive analysis to date of non-pharmaceutical interventions and sperm parameters, drawing on studies from different countries, healthcare settings and experimental practices.
The analysis compared the non-pharmaceutical interventions evaluated for male infertility.
open_questions: What direct effects do non-pharmaceutical interventions have on fertility, beyond their effects on sperm-quality measures?
Will larger trials confirm the reported effects of ω-3 fatty acid supplementation on sperm parameters?
How might additional evidence change the estimated effects of supplements and acupuncture?
future_directions: Conduct larger RCTs to verify the effects of the discussed supplements on sperm parameters and fertility.
Undertake further research on the direct effects of non-pharmaceutical interventions on fertility.
Standardize semen-detection reference standards in future research.
Further classify non-pharmaceutical interventions across the different types of male infertility.
study_design: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials (RCTs). PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE, China national knowledge infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang database, and Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 5 April 2023. Two researchers independently screened studies and extracted data; a third researcher resolved disagreements.

population.description: Men with infertility enrolled in the included RCTs. The article states that participants across the trials were aged 18–45 years.
inclusion_criteria: Randomized clinical trials evaluating non-pharmaceutical interventions and semen parameters.
exclusion_criteria: Studies available only as summaries without additional data.

statistical_methods: Network meta-analysis was conducted in STATA 14. Comparative effects were estimated as mean differences using a random-effects model, with significance set at p < 0.05 and a 95% confidence interval (CI). Subgroup analyses examined heterogeneity. Network diagrams represented intervention sample sizes by node size and the number of studies per comparison by line thickness. Interventions were ranked using SUCRA. Comparison-adjusted funnel plots, Begg’s test, and Egger’s test were used to assess publication bias.
follow_up: Treatment duration varied across trials; twenty-two studies lasted longer than three months.

main_findings.context: A total of 2508 records were screened. Comparative mean differences were estimated with a random-effects network meta-analysis.

tables.title: SUCRA rankings for the treatments across outcomes
tables.summary: The SUCRA rankings place Exercise first for pregnancy rate; ω-3 Fatty acid for sperm concentration; Acupuncture for total motility; and Lycopene for forward motility, sperm quality and sperm count. These rankings describe the ordering of treatments and do not, by themselves, establish statistically significant differences.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that acupuncture, exercise and several dietary supplements may improve pregnancy rate or sperm-quality measures in male infertility. Because evidence for some supplements and acupuncture comes from small samples and the findings are heterogeneous, larger RCTs are needed to verify their effects on sperm parameters and fertility.
narrative_summary: This systematic review and network meta-analysis compared non-pharmaceutical approaches to male infertility using randomized trials. Of 2508 screened records, 27 RCTs involving n = 4008 patients were included. The investigators assessed pregnancy rate and sperm concentration, total motility, forward motility, quality and count. Compared with placebo, Exercise was associated with a higher pregnancy rate (MD, 3.43 (95% CI, 2.05 to 4.82)). For sperm concentration, the reported advantages included ω-3 fatty acid (MD, 9.93 (95% CI, 7.21 to 12.65)), lycopene (MD, 8.79 (95% CI, 2.67 to 14.91)) and acupuncture (MD, 5.40 (95% CI, 2.32 to 8.49)). Acupuncture improved total motility relative to placebo (MD, 17.81 (95% CI, 10.32 to 25.29)); lycopene also showed an advantage (MD, 19.91 (95% CI, 2.99 to 36.83)). Lycopene ranked first for forward motility, sperm quality and sperm count, but the analysis did not find a statistically detectable advantage over placebo for the sperm-quality outcome. The authors regard these interventions as potentially useful for improving semen measures and male fertility. They caution that pregnancy depends on factors beyond sperm quality, semen-testing standards varied, and small samples and heterogeneity may change the estimated effects. They call for larger RCTs, including research on direct fertility outcomes.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: Infertility affects about 10% of the global population, and the WHO recognizes it as a worldwide public health problem. This network meta-analysis examined whether non-pharmaceutical interventions improve sperm quality, using randomized clinical trials identified in PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, China national knowledge infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang database, and Cochrane Library. For sperm concentration, ω-3 fatty acid, lycopene, acupuncture, and vitamin showed advantages, respectively: MD, 9.93 (95% CI, 7.21 to 12.65); MD, 8.79 (95% CI, 2.67 to 14.91); MD, 5.40 (95% CI, 2.32 to 8.49); and MD, 3.82 (95% CI, 0.70 to 6.94). Compared with placebo, total sperm motility improved with acupuncture (MD, 17.81 (95% CI, 10.32 to 25.29)) and lycopene (MD, 19.91 (95% CI, 2.99 to 36.83)). For forward sperm motility, the reported advantages were lycopene (MD, 8.64 (95% CI, 1.15 to 16.13)), Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) (MD, 5.28 (95% CI, 2.70 to 7.86)), acupuncture (MD, 3.95 (95% CI, 3.23 to 4.67)), ω-3 fatty acid (MD, 3.50 (95% CI, 2.21 to 4.79)), and vitamin (MD, 2.38 (95% CI, 0.96 to 3.80)). The authors conclude that acupuncture, exercise, lycopene, ω-3 fatty acids, CoQ10, zinc, vitamins, selenium, carnitine, and foods containing these supplements can improve sperm quality and may have a role in treating male infertility.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has characterized infertility as a major worldwide public health concern. Infertility means failure to achieve pregnancy after twelve months or more of appropriately timed intercourse without contraception. Approximately 10 to 15 percent of people worldwide are affected. Of approximately 186 million infertility cases worldwide, more than half involve male infertility. Studies have implicated reproductive-tract inflammation, irregular lifestyle, and nutritional deficiency in its development. Excess weight, alcohol abuse, metabolic syndrome, smoking, and environmental factors are strongly associated with poorer sperm quality and fertility; sperm quality can therefore influence ejaculate competitiveness and reproductive success. About 30–80% of male infertility is considered partly attributable to oxidative damage to sperm. Oxidative stress occurs when reactive oxygen species (ROS) exceed semen antioxidant defenses, damaging proteins, DNA, and lipids. The resulting sperm DNA injury can impair motility, the acrosomal membrane, and fertilizing ability, ultimately reducing fertility. An RCT suggested that resistance exercise might act through anti-inflammatory and antioxidant pathways. Management options include pharmaceutical, non-pharmaceutical, and surgical interventions. Drugs used clinically include antioxidants, hormones, hexanone theobromine, L-carnitine (LC), and other agents; the authors describe drawbacks involving unpredictable adverse effects, cost, dependence on individual circumstances, and unsatisfactory outcomes. Non-pharmaceutical approaches developed for male infertility include acupuncture, massage, moxibustion, and scraping. Lifestyle-focused approaches may improve sperm quality, motility, morphology, and men's overall physical fitness. Earlier systematic reviews, with or without network meta-analysis, evaluated treatment efficacy and safety but did not compare the effects of different non-pharmaceutical treatments. This study therefore aimed to compare their effectiveness for male infertility through network meta-analysis.

document_sections.heading: Data sources and searches
document_sections.content: For this network meta-analysis, the authors searched PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE, China national knowledge infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang database, and Cochrane Library for RCTs from database inception to 5 April 2023. The strategy combined free-text and medical subject terms concerning male infertility with terms for diet, exercise and exercise therapy, acupuncture and acupuncture therapy, and psychotherapy. Reference lists of retrieved articles, including relevant reviews, were also checked.

document_sections.heading: Study selection
document_sections.content: After duplicate records were removed, two independent researchers, ZMH and SJW, screened titles and abstracts for eligibility. Reports available only as summaries without additional data were excluded. ZHC was designated to resolve disagreements during screening and data extraction. The authors planned to depict study selection in a flow chart following PRISMA guidelines.

document_sections.heading: Data extraction and quality assessment
document_sections.content: Two researchers independently entered data from included reports into the same predefined Excel table, with disagreements referred to a third reviewer. Extracted information included first author, publication year, age, sample size, intervention, daily dosage, treatment duration, and outcomes. Pregnancy rate was the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes comprised sperm concentration, total motility, forward motility, quality, and count. The authors extracted the measures used by each included study to assess sperm parameters. Both fresh and cryopreserved semen were eligible; within each study, sample-collection conditions were the same in control and intervention groups. The authors considered the resulting influence on their conclusions minor.

document_sections.heading: Risk-of-bias assessment
document_sections.content: Two independent reviewers assessed risk of bias (ROB) for each result using the Cochrane ROB tool, with a third reviewer resolving disagreements. The article describes its RCT categories as low risk when suspected bias would significantly alter results, unclear when anticipated bias introduced uncertainty, and high risk when anticipated bias would completely change an outcome. A comparison-adjusted funnel plot was used to examine major publication bias.

document_sections.heading: Data synthesis and analysis
document_sections.content: The network meta-analysis (NMA) was conducted in STATA 14. Comparative effects were expressed as mean differences estimated with a random-effects model. Statistical significance was set at a p-value of < 0.05 with a 95% confidence interval (CI). Subgroup analyses across interventions were undertaken to investigate between-study heterogeneity. In network diagrams, node size represented the number of patients randomly assigned to an intervention, while line thickness represented the number of researchers assessing a comparison. The authors estimated the probability of each intervention occupying each rank and summarized the treatment hierarchy using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA). They defined a SUCRA value of 100 as certainly best and 0 as certainly worst.

document_sections.heading: Study characteristics
document_sections.content: Of 2508 records screened, 27 RCTs involving n = 4008 patients were included. Network diagrams covered pregnancy rate, sperm concentration, total motility, forward motility, quality, and count. The primary-outcome intervention set contained 11 options: CoQ10, zinc, ω-3 fatty acid, carnitine, selenium, lycopene, vitamin, zinc + vitamin, exercise, acupuncture, and placebo. Exercise, acupuncture, and vitamins each appeared in 4 trials. Acupuncture studies comprised acupuncture (2 trials) and electroacupuncture (2 trials). CoQ10, selenium, and zinc + vitamin each appeared in 3 trials. Table 1 summarizes study characteristics, regimens, treatment periods, and reported sperm outcomes. Twenty-two studies lasted longer than three months. The mean study size was 148 individuals, with a range from 8 to 521 patients. Across trials, patients were aged 18–45 years. Recruitment locations were Europe for Eleven (40.7%) trials, Asia for three (11.1%), North America for one (3.7%), Australia for one (3.7%), South America for one (3.7%), South Africa for one (3.7%), and the Middle East for nine (33.3%). The authors state that SUCRA rankings indicate benefit from all interventions relative to placebo and describe the comparison funnel plots as broadly symmetric.

document_sections.heading: Network meta-analysis
document_sections.content: Twenty-six studies were included in the assessment of non-pharmaceutical treatments and sperm quality. The RCTs commonly examined CoQ10, zinc, omega-3 fatty acids, carnitine, selenium, lycopene, vitamin, zinc + vitamin, exercise, and acupuncture. The authors considered the number of trials and their homogeneity sufficient for network comparisons of pregnancy rate and sperm concentration, total motility, forward motility, quality, and count. Network diagrams depict the available comparisons, with thicker lines indicating more included studies and larger nodes indicating larger samples.

document_sections.heading: Pregnancy rate
document_sections.content: Four studies contributed to the pregnancy-rate network meta-analysis. In Table 2, the three highest SUCRA ranks were exercise, zinc, and acupuncture. The authors describe acupuncture as significantly advantageous over placebo (MD, 1.68 (95% CI, −1.33 to 4.68)); zinc as more effective than placebo (MD, 1.90 (95% CI, −1.16 to 4.99)); and exercise as more effective than placebo (MD, 3.43 (95% CI, 2.05 to 4.82)). They report no detectable differences for the other comparisons.

document_sections.heading: Sperm concentration
document_sections.content: Twenty studies contributed to the sperm-concentration analysis. Table 2 ranks ω-3 fatty acid, lycopene, acupuncture, and vitamin highest by SUCRA. Against placebo, their respective advantages were MD, 9.93 (95% CI, 7.21 to 12.65); MD, 8.79 (95% CI, 2.67 to 14.91); MD, 5.40 (95% CI, 2.32 to 8.49); and MD, 3.82 (95% CI, 0.70 to 6.94). Compared with selenium, the respective differences favoring ω-3 fatty acid, lycopene, acupuncture, and vitamin were MD, 13.45 (95% CI, 6.48 to 20.42); MD, 12.31 (95% CI, 3.45 to 21.17); MD, 8.92 (95% CI, 1.83 to 16.02); and MD, 7.34 (95% CI, 0.22 to 14.47). ω-3 fatty acid and lycopene also performed significantly better than carnitine, respectively: MD, 9.81 (95% CI, 3.61 to 16.01) and MD, 8.67 (95% CI, 0.40 to 16.94). The authors additionally report statistically significant advantages for ω-3 fatty acid over acupuncture, vitamin, zinc + vitamin, and zinc, without giving effect estimates in this account. No other comparison showed a detectable difference.

document_sections.heading: Sperm total motility
document_sections.content: Sixteen studies informed the total-motility network. Acupuncture and lycopene occupied the top two SUCRA positions in Table 2. Relative to placebo, acupuncture had a significant advantage (MD, 17.81 (95% CI, 10.32 to 25.29)), as did lycopene (MD, 19.91 (95% CI, 2.99 to 36.83)). Acupuncture was also significantly better than ω-3 fatty acid (MD, 11.95 (95% CI, 0.38 to 23.52)), vitamin (MD, 13.72 (95% CI, 2.90 to 24.54)), carnitine (MD, 14.39 (95% CI, 1.99 to 26.78)), zinc (MD, 14.66 (95% CI, 1.43 to 27.89)), and zinc+vitamin (MD, 16.26 (95% CI, 3.20 to 29.32)). Other comparisons had no detectable differences.

document_sections.heading: Sperm forward motility
document_sections.content: Nine studies contributed to the forward-motility network. Lycopene, CoQ10, and acupuncture had the three highest SUCRA ranks in Table 2. Compared with placebo, forward motility favored lycopene (MD, 8.64 (95% CI, 1.15 to 16.13)), CoQ10 (MD, 5.28 (95% CI, 2.70 to 7.86)), acupuncture (MD, 3.95 (95% CI, 3.23 to 4.67)), ω-3 fatty acid (MD, 3.50 (95% CI, 2.21 to 4.79)), and vitamin (MD, 2.38 (95% CI, 0.96 to 3.80)). The authors found no detectable differences in the remaining comparisons.

document_sections.heading: Sperm quality
document_sections.content: Seven studies contributed to the sperm-quality network. Lycopene and selenium were the two highest-ranked treatments by SUCRA in Table 2. Despite those rankings, lycopene, selenium, ω-3 fatty acid, vitamin, and carnitine were not statistically better than placebo for this outcome. No other comparison showed a detectable difference.

document_sections.heading: Sperm count
document_sections.content: Seven studies informed the sperm-count network, in which lycopene ranked first by SUCRA in Table 2. Lycopene performed better than acupuncture (MD, 49.88 (95% CI, 11.66 to 88.10)), ω-3 fatty acid (MD, 50.06 (95% CI, 11.73 to 88.40)), vitamin (MD, 50.61 (95% CI, 10.71 to 90.51)), and placebo (MD, 62.05 (95% CI, 25.93 to 98.17)). No detectable differences were reported for other comparisons.

document_sections.heading: Quality assessment and publication bias
document_sections.content: Twenty-seven articles met the inclusion and exclusion criteria for the network meta-analysis. The authors assessed quality and publication bias using funnel plots, Begg’s test, and Egger’s test. They describe the funnel plot of logarithmic WMD as symmetric and interpret it as showing no significant publication bias.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: The authors characterize this RCT network meta-analysis as the most extensive assessment to date of non-pharmaceutical interventions and sperm parameters across countries, healthcare settings, and experimental practices. They interpret their findings as beneficial effects of exercise, zinc, and acupuncture on pregnancy rate; acupuncture, omega-3 fatty acids, lycopene, and vitamins on sperm concentration; acupuncture and lycopene on total motility; acupuncture, lycopene, and CoQ10 on forward motility; and lycopene on sperm count. They suggest other dietary supplements might also support male fertility. Improving semen quality and ultimately pregnancy rates is the goal of treating male infertility. The article cites RCTs that reported improvements in semen measures, pregnancy, and live birth with non-pharmaceutical approaches. It also cites studies associating diet, exercise, and acupuncture with fertility in women, and with endometrial thickness, embryo implantation, and live birth among women undergoing in vitro fertilization. The authors regard those findings as consistent with their observed positive associations of exercise, zinc, and acupuncture with clinical pregnancy rates. Assessment of an ejaculate's fertilizing potential includes sperm-function testing and examination of morphology, motility, concentration, viability, acrosomal reaction, and oocyte penetration. The authors describe semen-sample sperm-quality assessment as the standard way to evaluate potential fertility. Omega-3 fatty acids have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties and may influence membrane function through incorporation into cell membranes; the authors propose this as a possible explanation for effects on spermatogenesis. They cite evidence that successful fertilization depends on sperm-membrane lipid composition. Their analysis found a positive association between Omega-3 fatty acid supplementation and sperm concentration, but they call for additional large RCTs to confirm effects on sperm parameters. Lycopene is described as a potent antioxidant, an aliphatic hydrocarbon that protects against lipid peroxidation, and a substance reported at high concentrations in testes. The cited literature suggests a possible role in spermatogenesis, effects on biological processes in prostate disease, and protection against oxidative-stress-related testicular injury and sperm-quality changes. The authors consider acupuncture a possible treatment for asthenospermia and cite recent studies reporting efficacy across forms of male infertility. Discussed acupoints include Guanyuan, Qihai, Zusanli, Sanyinjiao, Baihui, and Yinlingquan. In the traditional framework presented, Guanyuan and Qihai relate to reproductive vitality; Sanyinjiao regulates the three Yin meridians, supports the spleen, addresses dampness, nourishes Yin and blood, and promotes circulation; Zusanli and Yinlingquan support the spleen and stomach and regulate Qi and blood; and Bai hui, associated with Dumai, supports Qi and Yang. The article proposes that combining these acupoints balances Yin and Yang, supports kidney essence, and promotes sperm growth, vitality, and pregnancy. A Norwegian study reported that about 20 percent of infertile men preferred alternatives such as acupuncture. Cited summary findings on concentration and motility suggested acupuncture could be used for oligozoospermia and asthenospermia. Siterman et al. proposed that acupuncture might reduce sperm lipid peroxidation or genital inflammation through increased immune responses; the authors consider their results consistent with prior acupuncture studies. CoQ10 is described as an antioxidant involved in electron transport. Balercia and Safarinejad et al. suggested that it suppresses organic peroxide formation in semen and might thereby reduce sperm oxidative stress. The authors propose that antioxidant activity could explain improvements in sperm quality and motility and note increasing interest in CoQ10 for fertility. They describe an overall improvement in sperm parameters in this study. They state that LC, L-acetylcarnitine (LAC), and their combination have been shown to increase sperm motility, while their analysis suggested some benefit of carnitine for concentration and total motility. Carnitine is described as participating in long-chain fatty-acid transport into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation and as potentially enhancing antioxidant enzyme expression. Cited research suggests carnitine therapy improves sperm function and fertilizing capacity. Zinc, selenium, and vitamins are identified as antioxidant supplements with reported benefits for sperm-quality parameters. Selenium is described as important to spermatogenesis and glutathione peroxidase-1 expression and activity; zinc as stabilizing membranes through inhibition of membrane-bound oxidases. A cited cross-sectional study associated greater vitamin C and E intake with higher sperm count and motility. The authors suggest their network analysis likewise indicates that zinc, selenium, and vitamin supplementation may improve sperm quality in infertile men. They cite the fifth edition of the World Health Organization's semen-quality standards, which gives a normal sperm-survival reference value above 58% and associates that value with a relatively high probability of pregnancy. They add that conception also depends on sperm count, concentration, motility, morphology, and seminal-plasma quality, and state that greater semen quantity and sperm quality correspond to greater pregnancy success.

document_sections.heading: Limitations
document_sections.content: Some non-English reports could not be reviewed because they could not be translated into commonly used languages; incorporating their results might change the analysis. Different subgroups in some studies made overall comparisons difficult. Excluding low-quality studies and conducting subgroup analyses partly addressed this issue but did not remove it. Although the authors found improvements in sperm quality, they say more research is needed on direct effects of non-pharmaceutical interventions on fertility. Pregnancy rate is affected by many factors besides sperm quality and, in their view, should not serve as the principal index or gold standard of clinical effect in male infertility. Semen-testing reference standards differed across research units, warranting more standardized studies. The diversity of infertility types and interventions also calls for further classification of non-pharmaceutical interventions. Despite these limitations, the authors consider the comparison of the available non-pharmaceutical interventions an important contribution.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSION
document_sections.content: The authors describe their work as the most extensive assessment to date of how non-pharmaceutical approaches—including acupuncture, exercise, foods, supplements, and nutrients—affect sperm-quality measures. They conclude that supplementation with antioxidants, particularly selenium, zinc, omega-3 fatty acids, CoQ10, and carnitine, alongside acupuncture, exercise, and foods rich in these supplements, can favorably affect pregnancy rate and sperm-quality parameters and influence male fertility. They caution that few studies of supplements and acupuncture were included, leaving small samples, and that findings were highly heterogeneous; further research may therefore change the meta-analytic effect estimates. They call for more RCTs with larger samples to verify effects on sperm parameters and fertility.
